report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity.
However, accurate and reliable epidemic forecasting remains notoriously challenging and is an evolving field in which new scientific advances continue to support forecasting efforts.
Computational models that underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models are promising developments that may improve seasonal epidemic forecasting.

This study aims to compare the performance of a selection of AI models previously identified as well adapted to epidemic forecasting, including machine learning (XGBoost), deep learning models (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer), time-series foundation model (Chronos), and a hybrid model: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), against statistical models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Prophet) and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM) in seasonal epidemic forecasting across Canada.
The study uses weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season as a test case.
Each model generated short-term (up to 5 weeks ahead) forecasts independently for each province from October 11, 2025, to March 28, 2026.
We evaluated performance using mean absolute error (MAE) for each province.

Our results show that AI models, specifically GRU, Transformer, and Chronos models, achieve lower MAE than CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan).
Meanwhile, CEM and ARIMA outperform all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia), respectively.

Furthermore, data pooling strategies that leverage multi-province data for the target virus or multi-virus data within individual provinces greatly improve deep learning models, and Chronos performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia.
In contrast, Prophet always has the highest MAE, and PINN is worse than CEMs.
Overall, AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs.
However, these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation.
We therefore conclude that AI models are best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs, which remain crucial for interpretability and informing decision-making.
Seasonal acute respiratory infections impose a recurrent burden on healthcare systems and contribute substantially to annual morbidity [1].
text.formatted: Seasonal acute respiratory infections impose a recurrent burden on healthcare systems and contribute substantially to annual morbidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: At the onset of each season, surveillance systems track the emergence of epidemic activity, signaling the early phase of an outbreak.

The progression of an epidemic is typically summarized using an epidemic curve, which represents the temporal evolution of indicators or targets such as incident cases, test positivity rates, hospital admissions, or infection-associated deaths.
Whether strictly seasonal or driven by other transmission dynamics, such epidemics often follow a broadly predictable trajectory.

In its simplest form, this trajectory consists of an initial phase of approximately exponential growth in incidence, followed by a peak as the pool of susceptible individuals becomes depleted, and subsequently a decline toward near-zero incidence.
Despite this typical shape, it is usually challenging to predict the epidemic trajectory accurately.
Therefore, the development of epidemic forecasting models is an active research area aiming to robustly forecast epidemic trajectories with satisfactory accuracy and confidence.

Forecasting models are commonly designed to generate predictions ranging from a few weeks to several months ahead (depending on the disease and/or the goal of the forecasts), as well as to estimate peak magnitude and peak timing.
As shown during multiple severe outbreaks, accurate forecasting models are essential for informing public health policy and operational planning [2].
text.formatted: As shown during multiple severe outbreaks, accurate forecasting models are essential for informing public health policy and operational planning <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, advance knowledge of epidemic trends enables policymakers to implement timely interventions, including situational awareness, vaccination campaign planning, expansion of healthcare capacity, and optimized resource allocation when peak timing and magnitude can be anticipated.
In the absence of reliable forecasting models, decision-making and interventions can be suboptimal, leading to substantial human and financial costs.

Several methodological approaches have been proposed for epidemic forecasting, among which compartmental epidemiological models (CEMs) provide a mechanistic framework for describing disease transmission dynamics.
CEMs are the most popular formulation, partitioning the population into relevant epidemiological states.

The progression of the epidemic occurs through transitions of individuals between those epidemiological states, for example using systems of differential equations (the canonical Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered model [3]) or computational rules (agent based models).
text.formatted: The progression of the epidemic occurs through transitions of individuals between those epidemiological states, for example using systems of differential equations (the canonical Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered model <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>) or computational rules (agent based models).

text.text: Machine learning algorithms underpinning "artificial intelligence" (AI) have had enormous interest from the scientific community over the past few years.
Indeed, they have rapidly achieved capabilities that open new possibilities in terms of support and implementation of scientific projects across various fields.
In particular, based on the promises of AI models, several groups have started to explore AI models to forecast epidemics [4, 5].
text.formatted: In particular, based on the promises of AI models, several groups have started to explore AI models to forecast epidemics <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5]</ref>.

text.text: We may be at a pivotal moment where AI models are becoming essential tools for epidemic modellers, with the potential to transform how epidemic forecasting is conducted.
In this study, we review traditional approaches to epidemic forecasting alongside recent advances in AI, with particular attention to their performance and applicability.

Using a concrete case study of seasonal influenza forecasting in Canada, we assess the predictive accuracy of selected AI models and compare their performance with that of established epidemiological models.
Importantly, our evaluation is grounded in a public health practice perspective.

Rather than focusing on highly specialized or experimental AI developments, we assess models as they would be encountered by public health professionals, i.e., scientifically trained users who can engage with methods and implementation at a high level but are not AI specialists.
Consequently, we focus on "ready-to-use" models, selecting those with accessible documentation, transparent methodologies, and user-friendly implementation.
This approach reflects a pragmatic and implementation-oriented view, aiming to bridge the gap between methodological innovation and real-world deployment in public health settings.

Finally, we identify and discuss the practical challenges that AI models may introduce for public health organizations, including issues related to usability, interpretability, and integration into existing workflows.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.

Section 2 provides background information and introduces the forecasting framework and baseline models considered in this study, including statistical, machine learning, deep learning, time series foundation, compartmental, and physics-informed neural network models.
It also presents a literature scan of AI models for epidemic forecasting.
Section 3 describes the study design, including the data and forecasting objective, training methodologies, data preparation and splitting, model training, and hyperparameter tuning.
Section 4 presents the experimental results, focusing on point forecast performance, followed by a discussion of the practical implications for public health applications.
Finally, Section 5 summarizes the main findings and discusses the practical challenges and considerations of using AI-based forecasting models in public health.
In this section, we briefly describe the forecasting process and models assessed in this study.
Readers are invited to read the Supplemental Materials for more details.
An epidemic curve can be represented as a time series, where observed incidence is periodically reported (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly, etc.).
We denote the observed incidence sequence by {y 1 , y 2 , . . . , y T }.

The forecasting task consists of predicting the next H future observed incidences, namely {y T +1 , . . . , y T +H }, where H and T represent the forecast horizon and total number of observations, respectively.
Formally, the forecasting task can be expressed as fitting, or "learning", a function f such that {y T +1 , . . . , y T +H } = f ({y 1 , . . . , . . . , y T }), where f is called a forecasting model.
Forecasts for a given horizon may be either deterministic or probabilistic.
Deterministic forecasts produce a single predicted value and are commonly referred to as point forecasts.
In contrast, probabilistic forecasts provide a predictive distribution or a set of quantiles, thereby characterizing uncertainty in future outcomes (Figure 1).
text.formatted: In contrast, probabilistic forecasts provide a predictive distribution or a set of quantiles, thereby characterizing uncertainty in future outcomes (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Ideally, forecasts should be accurate, stable, and, in the probabilistic setting, accompanied by well-calibrated and sufficiently narrow uncertainty intervals.
In this paper, we consider a diverse set of forecasting models.

Specifically, we consider compartmental mechanistic models (CEMs), statistical models, machine learning (ML) models, deep learning (DL) models, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), and time-series foundation models (TSFMs).
Furthermore, in order to compare all evaluated models, our primary focus is centered strictly on point forecasts as some models cannot natively generate probabilistic forecasts.
Before describing the individual models, we first explain how we transform a time series into training samples for models that require an explicit supervised-learning formulation.
Standard ML and DL models are inherently static; they expect tabular data with distinct feature vectors (X) and target vectors (y) and cannot process raw, continuous sequence data.
To bridge this gap, we use lag embedding (the sliding-window approach).

This approach converts a single long time series into training supervised samples (input-target pairs), where the feature vector consists of a window of p past observations and the prediction target is the next h future observations.
By framing temporal dependencies as static tabular features, lag embedding lets us cast sequence forecasting as a standard regression task and leverage powerful ML and DL algorithms.

Lag embedding, also called training sample creation, transforms a univariate time series into a supervised learning problem by using a sliding window of past observations as predictors and subsequent observations as targets.
For a given time series, a specified number of past observations form each input sample, while the following observation(s) form the corresponding forecasting target.
Moving the window through the time series generates a sequence of inputtarget pairs for model training.
This representation enables ML and DL models to learn temporal dependencies and patterns from historical observations.
The resulting samples are subsequently used to train the forecasting models.
Recursive forecasting produces multi-step-ahead forecasts sequentially, one step at a time.
The model predicts the next observation based on the latest available observations.
The model then re-injects the predicted value into the input sequence and uses it, along with the remaining recent observations, to generate the next prediction.
This is repeated recursively until the desired forecasting horizon is reached.
Thus, predictions from previous steps are used as input for subsequent forecasting steps.
Consider a univariate time series with 10 observations: y = [y 1 , y 2 , y 3 , y 4 , y 5 , y 6 , y 7 , y 8 , y 9 , y 10 ].

We construct supervised learning data using a lag order (window size or context length) p = 3, where each input x i consists of the previous three values of the series, and the target y i is the next value.
Thus, the time series is transformed into a supervised training dataset: 1 y 1 y 2 y 3 y 2 y 3 y 4 y 3 y 4 y 5 y 4 y 5 y 6 y 5 y 6 y 7 y 6 y 7 y 8 y 7 y 8 y 9
For models requiring lag embedding, the number of training samples generated from the original time series is T -p.
In the example above, with T = 10 and p = 3, this yields 10 -3 = 7 training samples.
This formulation provides a unified framework for predicting future incidence values from historical epidemic data.
Once the model is trained, it can be used for forecasting.
Assume that the last available input window consists of the observations [y 8 , y 9 , y 10 ].
For a forecasting horizon of H = 5, recursive forecasting proceeds by iteratively feeding predictions back into the model: ŷ11 = f (y 8 , y 9 , y 10 ) , ŷ12 = f (y 9 , y 10 , ŷ11 ) ,
In this approach, each predicted value becomes input for the next prediction step.
In the example above, we illustrate recursive forecasting, in which a single one-step-ahead model is iteratively applied to generate multi-step forecasts.
Some forecasting strategies instead train a separate model for each prediction horizon; this approach is known as direct forecasting.
In contrast, multi-output forecasting uses a single model to generate predictions for multiple future horizons simultaneously.
Some strategies also combine two or more of these approaches and are referred to as hybrid forecasting.

While ML and DL models require explicit lag embedding to construct input training samples, the statistical models and TSFMs handle lag-window construction and recursive multi-step forecasting internally.
Consequently, these architectures omit these preprocessing steps during feature engineering.
In contrast, CEMs and PINNs do not rely on lag embeddings or recursive forecasting.

Compartmental epidemiological models (CEMs) are the standard mechanistic models that are widely used for infectious disease modelling, and have their origin in the 1920s with the work of Kermack and McKendrick [6].

text.text: The fundamental features of these models are they i) compartment individuals of the population into epidemiological states, and ii) describe mathematically the migration dynamics of individuals between the compartments as the infections spread in the population.

The temporal evolution of compartment sizes is typically modelled using systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that describe transition rates between compartments, or equivalently, renewal equations [7].

text.text: One of the simplest compartmental models to simulate epidemics is the Susceptible-Infectious-Recovered ("SIR") model.

Individuals who have never been infected (i.e., still susceptible to infections) are grouped in the "susceptible" compartment, and the size of this compartment is noted S. Infectious individuals, their number is noted I, are grouped in the "infectious" compartment.
Finally, the "recovered" compartment (R) is filled with individuals who are no longer infectious and immune for life.

The CEMs can be designed to represent very complex epidemiological processes.

The practical limit to their complexity and size being the available data to fit the model parameters to and computational power (most CEMs are not analytically tractable and require numerical solvers).
CEMs are scientifically grounded as they mathematically represent biological and epidemiological processes underlying disease transmission and natural history, behaviors, and interventions.
These models are inherently interpretable and allow the estimation of key epidemiological parameters (e.g., basic reproduction number R 0 ).
They can also be used to assess the potential impact of public health interventions or behavioral changes on epidemic dynamics.
CEMs are often used to forecast infectious disease epidemics because they provide an attractive balance between modeling tractability and representativeness of the real world.

Forecasting is conceptually straightforward: once the model is fitted to observations, epidemic trajectories are simulated forward in time (beyond the last observation date) up to a predefined time horizon, constituting the forecasted epidemic.
The CEM used in this study is a simple SIR model implemented with a renewal equation, presented in Subsection 3.3.

text.text: Given that the primary audience for this report is public health practitioners, many of whom may have limited familiarity with AI models, this section offers a concise, high-level description of how they work.

AI models is a loose, umbrella term that generally refers to any computational model used to perform tasks associated with artificial intelligence, such as prediction, classification, generation, or decision-making.
Here, leaning on recent literature, we focus on modern models relevant to forecasting infectious disease epidemics.
In this paper, we focus on two categories of AI models: machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL).

Machine learning is a class of statistical and computational methods that learn patterns or relationships from data to make predictions, classifications, or decisions, without being explicitly programmed with fixed rules [24].
text.formatted: Machine learning is a class of statistical and computational methods that learn patterns or relationships from data to make predictions, classifications, or decisions, without being explicitly programmed with fixed rules <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Learning types are typically categorized by the amount of human/expert guidance provided.
In traditional machine learning, the three main types of learning are supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.

Supervised learning is a form of machine learning in which a model is trained on labeled data, that is, pairs of inputs and known outputs, to learn a mapping that can predict the output for new, unseen inputs.

In unsupervised learning, the model receives only unlabelled inputs and discovers patterns or structures, such as clustering similar data points, detecting anomalies, or reducing the dimensionality of complex datasets while preserving key information.
In this paper, we focus on supervised learning, specifically the regression task, as our goal is to forecast continuous variables (e.g., influenza incidence) rather than predict categorical labels.
Machine learning models have been widely applied to epidemic forecasting [25], with various models used for different forecasting tasks.

text.text: Decision tree regression is a non-parametric supervised learning method that models nonlinear relationships between input features and a continuous target variable.
The model recursively partitions the feature space into disjoint regions by selecting split points that minimize prediction error, typically measured using Mean Squared Error (MSE).
At each terminal node (leaf), the predicted output is the mean value of the training samples in that region.

text.text: To overcome this limitation, tree-based ensemble methods such as Random Forest and XGBoost combine multiple decision tree models to improve the predictive performance and robustness.

Given a set of training observations {(x i , y i )} m i=1 , XGBoost builds an ensemble of n decision trees and gives the prediction ŷi = n k=1 f k (x i ).
The k-th decision tree is indicated by f k .

text.text: In this setting, XGBoost learns a collection of small decision trees that capture simple patterns in the epidemic trajectory using only past case counts.
For example, Tree 1 may encode a rule such as: "if the number of cases in the previous week exceeds 100, then predict an increase in cases".
Tree 2 may capture acceleration, for instance: "if the number of cases last week is much higher than two weeks ago, then add an additional increase to the prediction".
Tree 3 may represent sustained growth, such as: if cases have been increasing over the last three weeks, then further amplify the forecast.
Each tree models a simple aspect of epidemic dynamics.
To make a forecast, the current observations, say 110 cases last week, 80 two weeks ago, and 60 three weeks ago, are passed through all the trees.

Each tree contributes a small numerical value (for example, Tree 1 predicts, say, +100, Tree 2 predicts +20, Tree 3 predicts +10), and the final prediction for the cases next week is obtained by summing contributions from all the trees (e.g., 130 cases for the next week in this simplistic example).
In this way, the model combines multiple simple rules derived from past epidemic behavior to produce an overall forecast.

Note that for real-world applications, more than hundreds of trees are generated, making the interpretation of the "discovered" rules by humans practically impossible (that is, outputs results are treated as a "black box").
To summarize simply, XGBoost forecasts an epidemic by learning how past case trajectories evolve, using many small decision trees that capture key patterns (like growth and acceleration).
XGBoost has been chosen on the basis of evidence from earlier forecasting studies.

Deep learning (DL) is a type of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with multiple layers to learn hierarchical data representations, allowing complex relationships and patterns to be modeled.

The Deep Neural Network (DNN) models [8, 12, 33, 34, 35, 36] employed in epidemic (short-term) forecasting are simple Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), BiLSTM, BiGRU, and transformers.

text.text: Artificial Neural Networks An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is a deep learning technique based on biological neural systems and comprises neurons connected and arranged in layers; it learns the relationship between inputs and outputs by modifying its weights and biases during training.
The neurons are the fundamental units of computation in an ANN.
Each one calculates a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias term, and then applies a nonlinear activation function.
Activation functions let the network model complex relationships by introducing non-linearity; without them, the network would function as a linear one no matter how deep it is.
An ANN consists of input, hidden (optional), and output layers: the input layer takes in the data, the hidden layers learn intermediate representations, and the output layer generates predictions.
A feedforward neural network is a network in which information flows in one direction through fully connected layers.
A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is a common example of a feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers and non-linear activations.
A deep neural network (DNN) is an MLP with many hidden layers to learn progressively more abstract patterns.
DNNs can learn complex nonlinear relationships and hierarchical representations from high-dimensional data.
Depending on the architecture, they can also capture temporal dependencies over different time scales.

In time series forecasting, these models act as static regressors, i.e., using a fixed window of past observations to predict future values, which means they lack memory and struggle to capture long-term temporal dependencies.

As a result, they are less suited to sequential data; hence, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants were introduced to incorporate memory by allowing time-dependent hidden states to accumulate information over time.

In this setting, a deep neural network learns a hierarchy of hidden representations from past epidemic data through multiple layers of neurons.

Assume the first layer learned that it needed to compute a simple weighted combinations to represent an overall level by applying weights of, say, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 to the number of cases of 1, 2 and 3 weeks ago respectively.
This first layer also needs to represent the recent increase signal by calculating the difference between the number of cases 1 and 2 weeks ago.

Assume the second layer can then combine these intermediate quantities, for instance detecting growth by amplifying the increase signal by a factor of , say, 1.2, and summing it with the overall level to produce an aggregate growth indicator.
A third layer may further transform this into a higher-level representation such as outbreak momentum, for example by scaling this signal by, say, 1.1.
These transformations are not explicit rules (unlike XGBoost) but learned numerical mappings.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks [37] are a type of RNN designed to overcome the "vanishing gradient problem" (i.e., when the network forgets how to learn from earlier information, because the updates become too tiny to have any effect) and capture long-range dependencies in sequential data.

text.text: They maintain two forms of memory, a long-term and a short-term, and use gating mechanisms to control what information is kept, updated, or discarded over time.
Gated Recurrent Units.
Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) [38] are a simpler version of LSTMs designed to handle the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs.

text.text: They use fewer gates (mainly an update gate and a reset gate) to control memory, making them faster and simpler while still capturing long-term patterns in sequential data.

Transformers.
The transformer architecture, introduced in [39], is a neural network architecture designed to handle sequential data efficiently that relies on "self-attention" mechanisms.

text.text: Transformers have revolutionized natural language processing and have been adapted for time series forecasting because they can model long-range dependencies and parallelize computations effectively.
The core of a Transformer is self-attention, which lets the model decide how important each time step is when making a prediction.
It does this by considering all the data at once, capturing the most important parts of the information, assigning weights to all inputs, and combining them into a contextual representation.

An encoder processes the input sequence, and a decoder uses this information to produce the forecast, while multi-head attention captures different types of relationships in the data simultaneously, making it particularly effective for complex time series forecasting tasks where multiple factors may influence the target variable.

text.text: In this context, so-called Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) [41, 42] have emerged as a promising solution, shifting from task-specific forecasting models to unified models that can generalize across fields such as epidemiology, finance, energy, and climate.

text.text: Like Large Language Models (LLMs) in natural language processing, TSFMs are pre-trained on large, diverse sets of time series data, which may reduce the need for extensive task-specific training.
TSFMs are trained on datasets that differ greatly in sequence length and temporal resolution, covering observations on a quarterly, monthly, weekly, daily, and hourly basis.
The datasets can contain real-world, synthetic, or hybrid time series drawn from a variety of domains as mentioned above.
Through pretraining, TSFMs learn general temporal patterns, such as trends, seasonality, and long-range dependencies, which can then be applied to downstream tasks or previously unseen datasets.
As illustrated in Figure 4, TSFMs generally operate through two stages: pretraining and adaptation.

text.text: During pretraining, researchers define a model architecture and train it on diverse time series using supervised or self-supervised learning.
Most TSFMs use transformer-based architectures, including encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder models, although non-Transformer architectures.
During adaptation, the pretrained model is tailored to a specific forecasting task or dataset to leverage the temporal representations learned during pretraining.
Common adaptation strategies include zero-shot inference, fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and tokenization-based [42].

text.text: We examine two adaptation methods: zero-shot and fine-tuning.
With zero-shot inference, we use the pre-trained model directly on the target dataset without further training, enabling us to assess its ability to generalize to previously unseen datasets.
This method is especially appropriate when historical data are scarce and offers a ready-made forecasting approach for various diseases, regions, and outcomes.
In fine-tuning, the pre-trained model is modified to suit the specific forecasting task by updating its parameters with task-specific data.
This finetuning process can involve updating all of the model's parameters or only some, leaving the rest unchanged.
In this study, we consider both parameter-efficient fine-tuning and full fine-tuning.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are neural networks that are trained not only on data, but also guided by known physical laws (like equations describing how a system behaves).
In simple terms, they learn from data while being constrained within the known rules of physics, so their predictions stay realistic (at least in the realm of what is physically possible).

In the context of epidemic models, using standard SIR model, the constraints can be driven by the dynamics of the subgroup population sizes (e.g., susceptible, infectious, recovered, etc.) and initial conditions.
For a more detailed discussion of PINNs and their applications to epidemic modeling and forecasting, we refer the reader to [48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54].

Although AI and machine learning models have been successfully applied to infectious disease forecasting, significant limitations continue to constrain their practical implementation.
First, interpretability remains a major challenge.

These models can produce accurate forecasts of disease dynamics but often provide limited insight into the mechanisms underlying their predictions, as they lack explicit mechanisms to depict how disease progression actually occurs.
This lack of transparency matters in epidemiological applications, where forecasts must be interpretable and actionable for policymakers and epidemiologists.

Moreover, purely datadriven models are not inherently grounded in epidemiological principles and therefore cannot directly provide scientifically meaningful quantities, such as the transmission rate or the basic reproduction number.
Second, their predictive performance and robustness depend heavily on data quality and availability.
This drawback is relevant for disease data, which are often sparse, under-reported, delayed, noisy, and over-dispersed.
Consequently, their performance may deteriorate, as is often the case for emerging or localized outbreaks.
AI models can learn spurious correlations rather than meaningful relationships, which may limit their ability to generalize to new outbreaks.
Finally, practical implementation presents significant operational hurdles.
Training and deploying these traditional AI models can be computationally expensive, requiring extensive hyperparameter tuning across high-dimensional parameter spaces.
Furthermore, successful implementation demands specialized technical expertise in machine learning engineering, and these architectures can struggle with long-term forecasting.
This study aims to assess the both the practicality and performance of selected AI models to forecast influenza A in the most populous provinces in Canada.

The choice for influenza A is motivated by the fact that this is a seasonal infection which has been part of the PHAC's respiratory viruses surveillance system for more than about two decades, hence there is a lot of data that can be leveraged by the models.

Moreover, seasonal influenza A is epidemiologically important because of its burden on health systems and global morbidity.
To summarize, seasonal epidemics of influenza A in Canada provide a good balance (for our study) between data quality, data quantity, season-to-season variability and public health relevance.

The exceptional growth of machine learning models underpinning "artificial intelligence" has driven a revolution in what science thought possible: large language models, protein-folding algorithms, and computer coding agents are just a few examples.

Hence, it is natural to apply these innovations in epidemiology, particularly to support efforts to lessen the impact of seasonal acute respiratory infections, which significantly strain health systems.

Hence, our study aimed to answer a simple question: as of 2026, can "AI" models forecast relatively standard seasonal epidemics, and can they outperform canonical compartmental epidemiological models (CEMs)?
As a concrete example, we chose to forecast influenza A in selected Canadian provinces.
To do this, we reviewed the literature and selected machine learning models that already yielded promising results in other studies.

After the literature review, we included one tree-based ensemble model (XGBoost), three deep learning models (LSTM, GRU, and Transformer), a physics-informed neural network (PINN) model, and one time-series foundation model (Chronos).

To compare these AI models with more traditional approaches, we chose an ARIMA model, a simple yet popular statistical approach; a more sophisticated statistical model, Prophet; and a SIR-like compartmental mechanistic model (CEM) used internally within PHAC to forecast seasonal respiratory infections over the past 5 years.
Short-term forecast accuracy for AI models was comparable to, and in select provinces marginally better than, traditional approaches; similarly, accuracy declined as the forecast horizon increased.
However, when accuracy was better, it was only marginally so, which ultimately does not really compensate for their limitations presented in subsection 2.10.

As a result, the expectation for the level of forecast accuracy should be much higher for AI models than for mechanistic models; in other words, to be practically useful, AI models should be much more accurate to compensate for their limitations (the main one being their intractability).

Additionally, we found that documentation for implementing AI models for non-expert users was minimal, if not lacking, for most AI models, consequently hampering their use by public health practitioners.

Furthermore, we note that the expertise required to run most AI models is currently relatively high, hampering adoption in most public health settings because they generally lack highly technical staff.

An important finding from our study is that while AI models could reach a similar or better accuracy than the CEM in half of the provinces (e.g., GRU, Transformer, and Chronos), the improvement was only marginal and, from a practical viewpoint, did not compensate for the opaqueness of AI models.

Indeed, public health practitioners need to understand the basic mechanisms behind a given forecast to explain the underlying epidemiology and, when forecasts are pessimistic, provide potential countermeasures to decision-makers.
Given their mechanistic nature, CEMs can disentangle all epidemiological aspects of a forecast, whereas AI models are largely inscrutable.
Although PINN models did not perform best in our study, they may be a promising approach in some cases.
This lower performance may stem from the simple SIR model it uses, or from the difficulty of tuning the loss weights.
Future work should thoroughly analyze how these loss terms affect PINN accuracy.
While TSFMs had a promising performance, Chronos achieved the best performance in British Columbia under zero-shot settings, demonstrating its utility without task-specific finetuning.
Nevertheless, we do not see Chronos systematically outperforming the best-performing models across all jurisdictions.

Future work should explore more TSFMs based on architectures (including transformer variants, i.e., encoder-decoder, encoder-only, and decoder-only, non-transformer models, and diffusion models), learning strategies (fully supervised vs. selfsupervised learning), and input representations (e.g., point-based vs. patch-based tokenization), as these factors may affect performance.
Synthesizing those factors will establish benchmark practices for epidemic forecasting.
In this work, we explored cross-domain generalization by pooling time-series data from multiple provinces and viruses (Influenza B, RSV, and COVID-19).

This data pooling significantly improved deep learning model performance, enabling globally and partially pooled architectures (such as GRU and Transformer) to outperform localized variants and achieve top ranks in multiple provinces.
Expanding cross-domain data pooling remains a critical avenue for future research in epidemic forecasting.
Despite the advantages of CEMs in providing insights into disease progression and their inherent interpretability, several limitations remain.
First, CEMs often rely on simplifying assumptions, such as homogeneous population mixing (even when the population is stratified), simplified contact patterns, or simplified pathogen evolution.
Second, model misspecification and partial observability may occur when the chosen CEM does not fully reflect real-world dynamics or when some compartments are not directly observable.
Third, epidemiological data are often sparse and uncertain because of under-reporting, testing limitations, and reporting delays, which complicates estimation of key model parameters.
These parameters are typically inferred from historical data that may change over time due to evolving public health policies, pathogen evolution, behavior change, etc.
Our study focused narrowly on the 2025/2026 influenza A season in selected Canadian provinces.
Hence, our results may not be generalizable to other settings or viruses.
Although we chose the Canadian setting out of interest, seasonal respiratory virus epidemic waves in Canada are similar to those in other temperate western countries.
Because AI models are datadriven, we expect similar findings if we applied our study to other similar geographical locations.

Forecasting influenza A, rather than other seasonal respiratory viruses, was chosen as we thought this virus provided a good balance of complexity: on the one hand, access to historical data of about 15 past seasons likely facilitated the fitting and training of the forecasting models; on the other hand, there is a marked heterogeneity between influenza A seasons (e.g., season start and peak timing, growth rate, etc.), likely caused mainly by the rapid evolution of this virus.
We attempted to leverage the AI models well.
However, our use may not have been optimal and may have impacted forecasting performance.
In future work should explore other supervised methods for generating samples, such as direct, multi-output, or hybrid models.

This study emphasized a practical approach: using AI models in a typical public health setting by professionals with a fair understanding of machine-learning theory and implementation, but who are not experts in this field.

Evaluating the 2025/2026 influenza A season across Canadian provinces shows that short-term forecast accuracy for AI models (such as GRU, Transformer, and Chronos) was comparable to or better than traditional models, and each model's accuracy declined as the forecast horizon increased.

The empirical findings yield key insights for AI deployment: cross-provincial and cross-virus data pooling help AI models to mitigate overfitting on small local sample sizes; AI models are slightly better than CEM, and zero-shot TSFMs like Chronos are also promising.
Conversely, models like Prophet or PINNs performed poorly.

An important finding from our study is that while AI models could reach similar or better accuracy than the CEM, the improvement was only marginal and, from a practical viewpoint, did not compensate for AI models' limitations.

Because public health practitioners require transparent, epidemiologically grounded forecasts to explain disease dynamics and justify interventions to decision-makers, mechanistic CEMs remain the most practical and reliable primary forecasting tool.
As AI models improve and become more widely used, they could play an important role in epidemic forecasting.
Further directions for investigation are numerous.
One approach is to develop hybrid methods that combine AI models with traditional models (statistical models and CEMs) to exploit their complementary strengths.
Alternatively, AI models can enhance CEMs by inferring their parameters from the observed data.
Such approaches could combine AI's predictive power with the interpretability and epidemiological structure of mechanistic models.
Another route is to use ensembling forecasts from different models to improve accuracy of forecasting.
Combining forecasts can reduce model-specific errors and improve robustness across provinces, forecast horizons, and epidemic seasons.

Unlike DNNs, RNNs explicitly model temporal dependence through recursive hidden states, allowing past observations to influence future predictions through memory.
Although RNNs use a hidden state to model temporal dependencies, they can struggle to capture long-range relationships due to the vanishing gradient problem.
As information is propagated through successive time steps, the influence of earlier observations diminishes, causing the hidden state to become increasingly dominated by recent observations.

Consequently, RNNs may have difficulty capturing long-term and periodic patterns in long sequences, motivating the use of gated architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs, which regulate the flow and retention of information.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks [37] are a specialized type of recurrent neural network (RNN) designed to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem that limits the ability of standard RNNs to learn long-range temporal dependencies.

text.text: The GRU architecture is computationally more efficient than LSTMs due to its reduced complexity, while still maintaining the ability to capture long-term dependencies in sequential data.

The update gate allows the model to adaptively control the flow of information from previous time steps, while the reset gate enables the model to forget irrelevant past information when generating the candidate activation.
This makes GRUs a popular choice for various sequence modeling tasks, including time series forecasting in epidemiology.
Although LSTMs and GRUs are effective at modeling long-term dependencies, they still rely on sequential processing of data, which can limit their efficiency when dealing with very long sequences.
This has led to the development of transformer architectures that leverage self-attention mechanisms to capture dependencies without relying on recurrent connections.
Another limitation of RNNs, including LSTMs and GRUs, is that they process sequences sequentially, which can lead to longer training times compared to feedforward models that can be parallelized.
This is particularly problematic for long sequences, where the computational cost can become prohibitive.
Transformers address this issue by allowing for parallel processing of sequence data, enabling more efficient training and better handling of long-range dependencies.
The transformer architecture, introduced in [39], is a neural network architecture designed to handle sequential data efficiently that relies on "self-attention" mechanisms.

text.text: Transformers have revolutionized natural language processing and have been adapted for time series forecasting tasks due to their ability to model long-range dependencies and parallelize computations effectively.
The core of a Transformer is self-attention, which lets the model decide how important each time step is when making a prediction.
It does this by considering all the data at once and aim to capture the most important parts of the information, assigning weights to all inputs and combining them into a contextual representation.

An encoder processes the input sequence, and a decoder uses this information to produce the forecast, while multi-head attention helps capture different types of relationships in the data at the same time, making it particularly effective for complex time series forecasting tasks where multiple factors may influence the target variable.

Prophet is a time series forecasting model developed for handling time series with multiple seasonal patterns, trend changes, and missing observations.
The model adopts a decomposable framework in which the observed time series is represented as the sum of trend, seasonal, and holiday components.
Prophet is particularly suitable for forecasting problems involving strong seasonality and nonlinear trends while maintaining interpretability and computational efficiency.

The global forecasting methodology follows the cross-learning (or data pooling) paradigm, in which a single forecasting model is trained on multiple related time series.
In this study, the global models leverage information from surveillance data collected across 8 Canadian provinces and three respiratory viruses (influenza A, Covid-19, and RSV).

Unlike local forecasting, where each model is trained independently for a single province and target virus, global models exploit shared temporal patterns and cross-series dependencies among different provinces and viruses to improve predictive performance.
Each time series is independently normalized using either Min-Max scaling or standardization.

The normalized series is then transformed into a supervised learning dataset via lag embedding, in which lagged observations serve as predictor variables and the subsequent observation is the target variable.
The lag-embedded matrices from all selected time series are vertically concatenated to form a single large training matrix.

Consequently, model training reduces to a standard supervised regression problem in which the predictor matrix consists of the lagged observations and the response vector contains the corresponding target values (see [73]).

text.text: In supervised learning, each input x i ∈ X has a corresponding target y i ∈ Y (y i = f * (x i ), f * is a function from an expert), and a learning algorithm learns a mapping f that predicts the output for new inputs; common tasks include classification (predicting discrete target, e.g., whether a disease is present in a region) and regression (predicting continuous values, e.g., disease incidence over time).
A learning algorithm (e.g., Gradient descent) learns the best f given the historical data.
The resulting model captures the relationship between the input and output, and is able to predict a target of an input.
In this work, we focus on regression, as forecasting aims to estimate a continuous future values.

In unsupervised learning, only inputs {x i } are given, and the model discovers patterns or structures f : X → Z, such as clustering similar data points, detecting anomalies, or reducing the dimensionality of complex datasets while preserving key information.

In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with an environment in state s t , takes actions a t , and receives rewards r t ; the goal is to learn a policy π : s → a that maximizes cumulative reward, as in adaptive epidemic interventions or game-playing applications.

Recurrent Units (GRUs) are a simplified variant of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks that also aim to address the vanishing gradient problem in standard Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).
GRUs combine the forget and input gates of LSTMs into a single update gate and use a reset gate to control the influence of previous hidden states on the current candidate activation.
This results in a more streamlined architecture with fewer parameters while still effectively modeling long-range dependencies in sequential data.
